traits: Black flies about 6-9 mm with a dull red thorax
Fly attached together in mating pairs
Two flights a year, roughly April-May and August-September
Splatter accumulates on car fronts and headlights

look_alikes.difference: Lovebugs have a red thorax and often fly stuck together in pairs; non-biting midges are smaller, mosquito-shaped, and don't pair up.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the body color and shape, and whether two individuals are joined together.

copy.what_it_means: Lovebugs are not known to bite or sting — they're a car-wash problem, not a pest-control problem, and no treatment prevents them since they drift in from miles around. The swarm season is short, typically about four weeks each flight.
copy.fact: Their body fluids are slightly acidic and can etch car paint if left baked on for several days — modern clear coats hold up much better than older paint.
copy.blurb: Lovebugs are a twice-a-year Florida nuisance that no treatment prevents — they drift in from miles around. The good news: they’re not known to bite or sting, and the swarm season is short.

tech_notes: No treatment; set expectations honestly — this is not a pest-control problem.

traits: Fuzzy, moth-like micro-fly, about 2.5-4.5 mm, resting on bathroom walls
Weak, hopping flight near sinks, tubs, and showers
Worse after a drain sits unused for a while
Larvae live in the gel-like film that builds up inside drains

look_alikes.difference: Drain flies are fuzzy and moth-shaped and stick to bathroom walls near drains; fungus gnats are slender, long-legged, and hover around houseplant soil.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the wing shape and where it was resting (drain vs. potted plant).

copy.what_it_means: The larvae live in the gel film that builds up inside drains, which is why a surface spray often misses the source. Clearing the drain film with a stiff brush and an enzyme-based cleaner is the usual approach; a technician can confirm the source if they keep coming back.
copy.fact: The larvae live in the gel film inside drains, not in the water itself — that's why the fix targets the film rather than the drain water.
copy.blurb: Cleaning the drain film (brush + enzyme cleaner) targets where the larvae actually live; a technician can confirm the source if they keep coming back.

tech_notes: Non-biting, no known disease transmission. Recommend mechanical drain cleaning; treatment is rarely needed if the source is addressed.

traits: Tiny dark flies with long legs and thread-like antennae, hovering around potted plants
Weak fliers that drift rather than dart
Larvae are slender, white, and legless in the top layer of wet potting soil
Numbers track soil moisture — more gnats means soil staying too wet

look_alikes.difference: Fungus gnats are slender and long-legged and hover over houseplant soil; drain flies are fuzzy and moth-shaped and stick to bathroom walls near drains.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the wing shape and where it was resting (potted plant vs. drain).

copy.what_it_means: It's an overwatering alarm with wings — the larvae need soggy soil to survive. Let pots dry out between waterings and yellow sticky cards will catch the stragglers; most cases need no treatment at all.
copy.fact: It's an overwatering alarm with wings — the larvae need soggy soil to survive.
copy.blurb: Let pots dry between waterings; yellow sticky cards catch the stragglers.

tech_notes: Harmless nuisance tied to overwatering; advise cultural fix (drying cycle) before any treatment.

traits: Dull gray fly with four faint dark stripes on the thorax
Large, reddish compound eyes that nearly touch on top of a male's head
Soft, sponge-like mouthparts used to sop up liquids, never to bite
Drawn to garbage, pet waste, and food left out, especially near kitchens and trash areas

look_alikes.difference: House fly has soft sponging mouthparts and never bites; the near-identical stable fly has a forward-pointing needle mouthpart and bites ankles
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in straight on at the front of the head showing the shape of the mouthpart.

safety_line: Can carry bacteria on its body from garbage or waste to food and counters; keep food covered and wipe down surfaces it has landed on.

copy.what_it_means: A very common nuisance fly that picks up bacteria from garbage and waste and can spread it to food and counters just by landing. Tightening up trash cans, pet waste cleanup and door seals is the main thing that helps with most house fly problems.
copy.fact: It can pick up and carry bacteria from dozens of different diseases just by walking across contaminated surfaces before landing on food.

tech_notes: Sanitation is primary control: trash storage/pickup, pet waste, exposed food/organic waste, door/window seals. Adulticide/fly bait per label for heavy pressure.

traits: Shiny metallic green, blue or copper body, noticeably more colorful than a house fly
Larger and heavier-bodied than a house fly, with a loud buzz
Drawn strongly to dead animals, garbage and pet waste rather than fresh food
Often the first fly to show up after something has died nearby

look_alikes.difference: Blow fly has a shiny metallic green, blue or copper body; house fly is dull gray with faint dark stripes and no metallic shine
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in under bright light showing whether the body has a metallic shine.

safety_line: Can carry bacteria from carrion or waste to food and counters; keep food covered and wipe down surfaces it has landed on.

copy.what_it_means: A shiny, metallic fly that shows up fast around garbage, pet waste or anything dead, often within minutes. A sudden cluster of them indoors, especially in an attic or wall, is worth checking for a dead animal in that area.
copy.fact: It can smell decaying matter from a very long distance and is often one of the first insects to find a carcass, which is why it is so useful to forensic investigators.

tech_notes: Indoor clusters, especially near attic/wall voids, can indicate a dead rodent or animal in that space; inspect before treating. Otherwise sanitation (garbage, pet waste) is primary control.

traits: Tiny tan to light brown fly with bright red eyes
Slow, hovering flight around fruit bowls, trash cans and recycling bins
Shows up fast around overripe or rotting produce, empty cans and sugary spills
Can also breed in drains and disposals if organic buildup is present

look_alikes.difference: Fruit fly has bright red eyes and flies in slow hovering loops; phorid fly has a humped back and tends to run rapidly across surfaces instead of flying off
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up showing eye color, or a few seconds watching whether it runs or flies when disturbed

copy.what_it_means: A tiny fly that breeds fast in overripe fruit, empty bottles and cans, and drains, going from egg to adult in about a week. Cleaning out the breeding source, not just swatting the flies you see, is what ends an infestation.
copy.fact: It can complete its entire life cycle from egg to adult in about a week in warm weather, which is why numbers can explode from just one forgotten piece of fruit.

tech_notes: Locate breeding source (overripe produce, recycling, drains/disposal buildup) rather than treating adults alone; sanitation resolves most cases without product application.

traits: Tiny fly with a noticeably humped, arched back over the thorax
Runs rapidly across counters and surfaces instead of taking flight right away
Breeds in a wide range of decaying organic matter: drains, garbage, rotting produce, even dead animals
Similar size to a fruit fly but darker and less red-eyed

look_alikes.difference: Phorid fly has a humped back and tends to run across surfaces when disturbed; fruit fly has bright red eyes and flies off in slow loops instead of running
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up showing the shape of the back, or a few seconds watching whether it runs or flies when disturbed

copy.what_it_means: A small fly that breeds in almost any decaying organic matter, from clogged drains to rotting food to, rarely, a dead animal in a wall. Persistent indoor numbers are worth tracking to their breeding source rather than just swatting the flies you see.
copy.fact: Its habit of running fast across a surface instead of flying off right away is one of the easiest ways to tell it apart from a fruit fly at a glance.

tech_notes: Very broad breeding range (drains, garbage, decaying matter, occasionally carrion); persistent indoor presence with no obvious kitchen source warrants checking for a dead animal in a void. Sanitation/source removal is primary control.

review.notes: Could not load a UF/IFAS EENY page dedicated to this exact species (Megaselia scalaris); IFAS source found (IN1144) covers a related agricultural Megaselia use case rather than the household nuisance angle.

traits: Sleek, dark, wasp-like fly, but with only two wings and no stinger
Two small, translucent 'window' patches near the base of the abdomen, giving it a pinched-waist look
Pale, whitish tips on the back legs
Larvae are found in compost, manure or rotting organic matter, not in clean food

look_alikes.difference: Black soldier fly has two wings and small clear window patches near the abdomen base; the wasp has four wings, a visible stinger and no window patches
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in counting the wings and checking for translucent patches near the base of the abdomen.

copy.what_it_means: A wasp-mimicking fly that isn't known to sting or bite people and whose larvae actually help break down compost and food waste. Its loud buzz and wasp-like look often worry people more than the insect itself warrants — it's best left alone.
copy.fact: Its larvae are so good at breaking down food scraps that they are now farmed commercially as a way to recycle food waste.

tech_notes: Beneficial decomposer; no treatment needed. Larvae in compost/organic waste are beneficial, not a pest issue.

review.notes: Verdict changed from harmless to ally: it's a beneficial decomposer, not just an inert visitor, so role beneficial / verdict ally fits better. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Looks like an oversized mosquito, but with a stouter body and no biting mouthparts
Very long, thin, stilt-like legs that detach easily if grabbed
Weak, fluttery flight and often just rests on walls or screens
No biting mouthparts, and doesn't hunt other insects despite the 'mosquito hawk' nickname

look_alikes.difference: Crane fly has extremely long, thin, stilt-like legs and a slender body with no biting mouthparts; gallinipper has short, sturdy, hairy legs and bites hard
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the legs showing whether they are extremely long and thin, or short and stout.

copy.what_it_means: Despite the 'mosquito hawk' nickname, this giant-looking mosquito lookalike has no biting mouthparts and doesn't hunt real mosquitoes. It's harmless to have around, and fine to just let it fly back outside.
copy.fact: Its long legs are built to snap off easily as a defense, which lets it escape a predator's grip by leaving a leg behind.

tech_notes: No biting mouthparts; not a health or nuisance-biting concern despite its size and mosquito-like look. No treatment needed for adults.

review.notes: Larvae (leatherjackets) can occasionally feed on grass roots elsewhere in the US, but this is not established as a significant SWFL turf issue; kept scope to the adult, which is the form usually photographed indoors/on screens. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Looks like a slim mosquito but has no biting mouthparts at all
Often shows up in huge swarms near porch lights, especially close to lakes, ponds or retention ponds
Rests with front legs held up and out, unlike a mosquito's low resting posture
Large die-offs can leave piles of dead insects on porches, cars and windowsills

look_alikes.difference: Non-biting midge holds its front legs up and out and has no biting mouthparts; southern house mosquito rests low, flat to the surface, and bites readily
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from the side showing how the front legs are held while resting.

safety_line: Doesn't bite or spread disease, but large swarms and dead-insect buildup can bother people with asthma or insect allergies.

copy.what_it_means: A non-biting insect that breeds by the millions in nearby lake or pond mud and swarms toward lights, especially near the water. Numbers depend on the whole waterbody, not just one yard, so cutting back unnecessary outdoor lighting near the water helps more than yard treatment.
copy.fact: Despite looking just like a mosquito, it has no functional biting mouthparts at all and cannot feed on blood.

tech_notes: Source is regional (lake/pond sediment), not the individual property; residential treatment has limited effect. Reducing exterior lighting facing the water is the most practical homeowner-level step.

traits: Yellow-and-black or brown-and-yellow striped body that mimics a bee or wasp
Only one pair of wings, unlike a real bee or wasp's two pairs
Hovers nearly motionless in midair near flowers before darting to a new spot
Larvae of many species are small, slug-like maggots that actively hunt aphids on plants

look_alikes.difference: Hover fly has one pair of wings, hovers still in place, and has no stinger; yellowjacket has two pairs of wings, flies more erratically, and can sting
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in checking wing count and whether it hovers motionless versus flying erratically.

safety_line: Looks like a bee or wasp but has no stinger to sting with, and doesn't bite people either.

copy.what_it_means: A harmless bee mimic that pollinates flowers as an adult, and many species have aphid-eating larvae as a bonus. There's no stinger and nothing to treat here.
copy.fact: Its bee-like colors are just a bluff for protection; it has no way to sting even if it wanted to.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; reassure customers this is a bee/wasp mimic with a single pair of wings and no stinger.

traits: Elongated, often bristly fly with a dense tuft of stiff bristles ('mustache') on its face
Large eyes that bulge out on either side of a notched top of the head
Ambushes and grabs other flying insects in midair, including wasps, bees and even dragonflies
Rests on fence posts, plant tips or bare ground, darting out after passing prey

look_alikes.difference: Robber fly is a true fly with one pair of wings and a bristly face; wheel bug is a true bug with a distinctive gear-shaped crest on its back
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the back checking for a wheel/gear-shaped crest versus a bristly face and single wing pair.

safety_line: Its bite is sharp and can really hurt for a bit if it's handled, but it isn't dangerous and only happens if it's grabbed.

copy.what_it_means: A skilled aerial predator that helps thin out other flying insects, including some real pests. It won't come after a person, and only bites defensively if it's caught and held.
copy.fact: It's bold enough to tackle insects much better armed than itself, including wasps, bees and dragonflies, snatching them right out of the air.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; beneficial predator. Advise not to handle it bare-handed to avoid a defensive bite.

review.notes: Per audit item 40: role changed from nuisance to beneficial and verdict from watch to ally, since the copy/tech_notes already describe it as a beneficial predator (validator requires verdict ally when role is beneficial). Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.
